page_lead: This page summarizes common childbirth practices and typical hospital expectations in Japan using titles and details.
item_1_detail: In Japan, vaginal delivery is the most common method. Cesarean section and epidural delivery are also available, but the way they are handled differs depending on the hospital.
item_2_title: What to confirm if you hope for epidural delivery
item_2_detail: Hospitals that offer epidural delivery are limited. In many cases, advance booking is required. If you are interested, it is best to confirm with the hospital early in pregnancy.
item_3_detail: Once pregnancy is confirmed, it is common to visit a hospital as early as possible. With a standard schedule, many people have about 14 prenatal checkups during pregnancy, but the number may vary depending on the course of the pregnancy and the hospital's policy.
item_4_detail: Many municipalities provide prenatal checkup tickets or coupons. Using them can reduce part of the cost of checkups. The way they are used and the amount covered differ by municipality.
item_5_title: Who can attend the birth and possible restrictions
item_5_detail: Some hospitals restrict who may be present during childbirth. Whether a husband, partner, or other family member may attend depends on the hospital, so advance confirmation is necessary.
item_6_detail: For vaginal delivery, many hospitals guide first-time mothers to stay about 5 days and mothers who have given birth before to stay about 3 to 5 days. This may change depending on the mother's condition, the baby's condition, and hospital policy.
item_7_detail: During hospitalization, breastfeeding guidance and baby bathing guidance are often provided. The exact content and number of sessions vary by hospital, but it is common to receive explanations to prepare for life after discharge.
item_8_detail: Nurses are medical and nursing professionals. They are not people who do every personal task in place of the patient. You can ask for help when needed, but the extent of support depends on the hospital system.
item_9_title: Restrictions on visiting hours and number of visitors
item_9_detail: Some hospitals limit visiting hours and the number of visitors. These rules vary depending on infection control measures and ward management policies, so it is important to check in advance.
item_10_detail: Nurses may sometimes help with taking photos as a kind gesture, but hospitals do not always have a dedicated photographer. If you want photos, check the hospital rules and attendance conditions in advance.
item_11_title: The custom of taking the umbilical cord home
item_11_detail: In Japan, there is a custom of taking the baby's umbilical cord home as a keepsake. Some hospitals give it to the family in a small box, but this depends on the hospital.
item_12_detail: Religious considerations and religion-based meal support differ by hospital. Many hospitals can provide allergy-friendly meals, but hospitals that can also respond to religious dietary restrictions may be limited. If you have requests, please consult the hospital in advance.
item_13_title: Rounds and interviews during postpartum hospitalization
item_13_detail: After childbirth, it is common to have daily rounds or examinations during hospitalization. In addition, doctors and nurses may ask about your condition through interviews.
item_14_title: The custom of the belly band on the Day of the Dog
item_14_detail: In Japan, there is a custom of wearing a belly band around the fifth month of pregnancy on an auspicious Day of the Dog to pray for a safe birth. It is not mandatory, but some people value it as a family event.
item_15_title: Where to submit the birth registration
item_15_detail: The birth registration must be submitted to the city, ward, town, or village office within 14 days of the baby's birth. Hospitals do not always have a government branch office inside, so it is good to prepare for a separate visit to the municipal office.
item_16_title: How to travel to the hospital when labor begins
item_16_detail: Some hospitals do not recommend coming by private car when labor begins. In some areas, labor taxi services are available, so it is reassuring to check transportation options in advance.
item_17_title: Use of a personal seal at admission
item_17_detail: Some hospitals require a personal seal for admission procedures. Recently, some hospitals no longer require one, but you should always check the admission instructions.
item_18_detail: Okuizome is a celebration held around the baby's 100th day, with the wish that the child will never have difficulty finding food. It is usually a family event and not something done at the hospital.
item_19_detail: A newborn home visit is a system in which a municipal public health nurse or similar professional visits your home after the baby is born. You can ask about the baby's condition and child-rearing concerns.
item_20_detail: After childbirth, there is often a one-month checkup for the mother, and municipalities may also provide guidance for infant checkups. For example, a 3-to-4-month infant checkup is common, but the timing and number of visits vary by municipality.
item_21_title: Rules for riding in a car with a baby
item_21_detail: When placing a baby in a car, you must use a child seat that matches the child's age and body size. In Japan, the use of child seats is required by law for children under six years old.
